messages.subject: Help troubleshoot multi-state model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would appreciate any help with troubleshooting code to fit a multi-state model. Please review the rmarkdown html attached.

The model is a linear sequence first, but may add sequences to make it multi-state. I loaded the following libraries:
library(INLA)
library(INLAjoint)
library(DiagrammeR)
library(tidyverse)

In brief, I simulated data of 100 patients per each insurance type (2 types total) and want to test the impact of insurance:
meddat<-tibble(time1=rexp(n=100,rate=log(2)/15),time2=rexp(n=100,rate=log(2)/10),time3=rexp(n=100,rate=log(2)/50),time4=rexp(n=100,rate=log(2)/50),insurance="medicare",event1=1,event2=1,event3=1,event4=1)

comdat<-tibble(time1=rexp(n=100,rate=0.8*(log(2)/15)),time2=rexp(n=100,rate=.8*(log(2)/10)),time3=rexp(n=100,rate=.8*(log(2)/50)),time4=rexp(n=100,rate=.8*(log(2)/50)),insurance="commercial",event1=1,event2=1,event3=1,event4=1)

tot.dat<-rbind(meddat,comdat)
glimpse(tot.dat)

Then, manipulated data to have cumulative sum of event times:
event<-matrix(c(tot.dat$event1,tot.dat$event2,tot.dat$event3,tot.dat$event4),ncol=4)
times<-t(apply(tot.dat[,1:4],1,cumsum))
tot.dat1<-cbind(times,tot.dat[,5:9])
glimpse(tot.dat1)

#########
Then I fitted a model:
#fit model
inlasurvmod<-joint(formSurv=list(inla.surv(times1,event1)~insurance,
                    inla.surv(times2,event2)~insurance,
                    inla.surv(times3,event3)~insurance,
                    inla.surv(times4,event4)~insurance),
      basRisk=rep("weibullsurv",4),data=tot.dat1)

### The error I receive is:
Error in joint(formSurv = list(inla.surv(times1, event1) ~ insurance, : argument 3 matches multiple formal arguments

Apologies if there is an obvious mistake. I am working through an example by Alvares et al. 2024 (http://arxiv.org/abs/2212.01900). Is it also possible to model sojourn times?

Best,
Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Help troubleshoot multi-state model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

You need to set the argument name to "dataSurv" instead of "data" as INLAjoint also deals with longitudinal models, thus it has both "dataLong" and "dataSurv" arguments instead of "data". Also in the survival outcomes you have to fix the name of the time columns (i.e., time without an s).
You can use the "truncation" argument in inla.surv to start the at-risk period at a specific time for each transition.

Best,
Denis Rustand
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: 2^31-1 byte limit
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

My dataset has 40,937,390 data points, each representing bird migratory stopover density in a 1km x 1km cell in a year. I am fitting an spde model of migratory stopover and I get the error:

 *** inla.core.safe:  The inla program failed, but will rerun in case better initial values may help. try=1/1
Warning in iinla(model = info[["model"]], lhoods = info[["lhoods"]], options = info[["options"]]) :
  iinla: Problem in inla: Error in paste0(vapply(x, function(x) { :
  result would exceed 2^31-1 bytes
iinla: Problem in inla:
iinla: Giving up and returning last successfully obtained result for diagnostic purposes.

When I aggregate the data to 4km x 4km cells, it fits fine.

I think the the 2^31-1 byte limit is imposed by R on character vectors, in which case increasing the memory and processing power of the computer wouldn't help.

Is there anything about the mesh or the model components that I could change to reduce the size of the character vector that inla has to save while fitting the model?

Thanks in advance for any help!

My mesh is made as folllows (units are km):
mesh =fm_mesh_2d_inla(boundary = list(radar_buffer_80_ag), max.edge = c(25, 500), offset = 500, crs = fm_crs(data))

And this these are the model components and formula:
# components
svc_components <- ~ -1 +
  alpha(cell, model = "iid", hyper = list(prec = pc_prec), constr = TRUE) +
  kappa(geometry, model = spde)

# formula
svc_formula <- stopover ~ .

#fit
res_1 <- bru(
  svc_components,
    like(formula = svc_formula,
    family = "gamma",
    data = data
    ),
  options = list(
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, cpo = FALSE),
    control.inla = list(
      int.strategy = "eb"
    ),
    verbose = TRUE,
    bru_verbose = 4
  )
)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think the 2^31 message may be due to a bug in the error reporting code and that the actual error is something else. The error reporting code has been updated in the development versions, so try installing fmesher and inlabru from github or the inlabru r-universe repository. Then run your code again to hopefully get a different error message.

I'm on holiday this week, so if the real problem is in inlabru itself I can't help more until next week.

Finn

messages.subject: No DIC for zeroinflatedbinomial model?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm starting to build a really basic spatio-temporal model to look at presence/absence of disease outbreak. My data is quite zero inflated, so have been trying to work with different model families to resolve this. One of the issues that I've been facing is that when I specify the model family as zeroinflatedbinomial1, no DIC appears even if its specified. This doesn't appear to be an issue using binomial or zeroinflatednbinomial1, but I wasn't sure if this was specific to the model family or if an error in my R coding.

Here is the model formula that I'm using, happy to provide more code or info if need be

formula_spatiotemp <- outbreak_occur ~ year +
  f(month, model = "ar1", cyclic = TRUE) +
  f(ID, model = "bym2", graph = ken.adj, scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE)

model_spatiotemp <- inla(
  formula_spatiotemp,
  data = monthly_data,
  family = "zeroinflatedbinomial1",
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE)
)

Thanks!

messages.subject_clean: Data fusion from INLA to inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA community,

I'm trying to fit a simple SPDE-based data fusion model using the inlabru syntax. The assumption is that, at the areal level, we observe an average (stochastic integral) of an underlying continuous variable.

I can fit the model using the INLA "tag" syntax. However, when I tried to switch to inlabru with the `bru_mapper` syntax, I got the following error:
#> Warning in fm_onto_mesh(mesh, loc, crs = crs): Unclear if the 'loc' class
#> ('numeric') is of a type we know how to handle.
#> Error in matrix(is.na <http://is.na>(as.vector(loc)), nrow = nrow(loc), ncol = ncol(loc)): non-numeric matrix extent

I'm clueless about how to deal with this error. Moreover, I cannot tell from the documentation whether what I am doing with the `bru_mapper` syntax is correct.

Any input would be very much appreciated.

A script with a minimal reproducible example is attached to this email.

Best,
Lucas.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lucas,

I would like to call your attention to a methodological detail in doing the integration of the continuous process over each area when modeling (the risk of) a counting process . There are people who do it at the linear scale (attempt 2 in the attached picture). Some even do attempt 1 still. However, the *right* is to integrate it at the risk scale. It is possible to do this with inlabru using the bru_mapper_logsumexp(), as exemplified in section 5 (pay attention to eq. in page 21) of https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00791 with the method developed in https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10584

Regards,
Elias

Hi Elias and Finn,

Thanks for sharing, Elias. Such a cool application of Jensen's inequality.
The link function for the data I'm working with is the identity, so that would not be a problem. But it is good to know that inlabru can handle that as well.

I was passing the geometry to the component. However, the way I was using the mapper was wrong. The examples from the paper Elias shared were enlightening and I was able to achieve what I was trying to.

In case someone faces the same problem, here goes what I was doing wrong. The code that was not working was as follows:
agg_mapper <- bru_mapper_aggregate(
    rescale = TRUE,
    n_block = NROW(my_dt)
)

cmp <- y ~
  my_sp(geometry,
        model = my_spde,
        mapper = agg_mapper,
        blocks = blocks) +
  my_intercept(1)

fit_bru <- bru(cmp, bru_dt, family = "gaussian")

Replacing it by the following does the trick:

agg_mapper <- bru_mapper_aggregate(
    rescale = TRUE,
    n_block = NROW(my_dt)
)

cmp <- ~ 0 + my_intercept(1) +
  my_sp(geometry,
        model = my_spde)

fml <-
  y ~ ibm_eval(
      agg_mapper,
      input = list(weights = weight, block = .block),
      state =  my_intercept + my_sp
  )

ips <- fm_int(my_mesh, samplers = my_dt)

lik <-
  like(formula = fml,
       family = "gaussian",
       data = ips,
       response_data = my_dt,
       allow_combine = TRUE)

The main problems were: (1) I was not using the fm_int function, and (2) I was not aware of how to use the ibm_eval function.

Thank you both.
Lucas.

messages.body_plain:
Hi
I am writing in this post, as my question is similar.
In my case, I need to code more than one random slope for spatiotemporal model, for predicting health outcome based on lagged observations as well as some climate variables.
Reading through the example given here, I coded my formula and model as below:
##############################################
f <- obs  ~ obs_lag1 +  obs_lag2 +  season + tas_lag1 + dtr_lag1  + season +
  f(ID.area, model="iid") + ## spatial random effect
  f(ID.month, model = 'iid')+ ## temporal random effect
  f(ID.area.month, model = 'iid') + ## space-time random effect
  f(ID.tas, tas_lag1, model = 'iid') + ## random slope for  tas_lag1 variable
  f(ID.dtr, dtr_lag1, model = 'iid') + ## random slope for  dtr_lag1 variable

model <-  inla(f,
                   family = "nbinomial", data = data.valid, E=popn,
                   control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, cdf=c(log(1)), link =1),
                   control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE),
                   control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0.0001), ##
                   control.inla=list(strategy="simplified.laplace")
)
summary(model)
##########################################
The assumption I would like to capture here is that the effect of climate variables (tas_lag1 + dtr_lag1 ) on health outcome will be different depending on the region.
 As each region has different climate conditions.

I am unsure if the above formulation captures this assumption, or whether I need to use a grouped effect as discussed here in Section 3.5.5 (https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-mixed.html)
The code runs fine, but I am getting very large precisions for some random terms.

Thank you
Aminath

messages.subject: spatiotemporal model with dynamic covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm working on a marine integrated species distribution model (ISDM) using inlabru and the PointedSDMs wrapper. My model combines two data sources:

Presence-Only (PO) Data:
Collected over 12 months, this dataset is highly spatially biased but provides valuable temporal information on dynamic covariates (temperature).

Presence-Absence (PA) Data:
Derived from a survey (1 month)  with good spatial coverage, providing static covariates such as bathymetry and slope.

My goal is to build an integrated model that incorporates bathymetry and slope from the PA data and temperature from the PO data, in which I want to model PO as an IPP and PA Binomial. To test whether the model can capture the dynamic distribution driven by temperature variations, I’m currently focusing on modelling only the PO data.

In my workflow, I define the temporal component by including a "month" variable in the PO dataset. In the startISDM() call, I specify the temporal variable as follows:

organizedData_PO <- startISDM(
  data = po_sf,
  Mesh = mesh,
  Projection = proj_azores,
  spatialCovariates = env_stack_bst_masked,
  Boundary = boundary_inner_PO,
  responseCounts = "counts",
  pointsSpatial = "individual",
  temporalName = "month"
)

For temperature, I combine the 12 monthly layers into a dynamic component using changeComponents(): (I also use a 1D SPDE for temperature to capture a non linear response)

organizedData_PO$changeComponents(
  "temperature(
     main = I(
      (month == 1)*temperature_month1 +
      (month == 2)*temperature_month2 +
      (month == 3)*temperature_month3 +
      (month == 4)*temperature_month4 +
      (month == 5)*temperature_month5 +
      (month == 6)*temperature_month6 +
      (month == 7)*temperature_month7 +
      (month == 8)*temperature_month8 +
      (month == 9)*temperature_month9 +
      (month == 10)*temperature_month10 +
      (month == 11)*temperature_month11 +
      (month == 12)*temperature_month12
     ),
     model = INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(
       mesh = fmesher::fm_mesh_1d(
         loc      = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 20),
         boundary = 'free'
       ),
       alpha       = 2,
       prior.range = c(1, 0.05),
       prior.sigma = c(1, 0.05),
       constr      = TRUE
     )
  )"
)

However, I'm not entirely sure if this is the most elegant or robust way to link the temporal "month" variable from the PO sf to the dynamic temperature SPDE fields. I am wondering:
Is specifying temporalName = "month" in startISDM() sufficient for linking the month-specific temperature layers to the PO data? (this question might be limited to users of the package)
Are there any resources or example cases available where others have used temporally changing covariates in spatiotemporal models in INLA? (I am aware of a few examples using spatiotemporal models but not with temporally explicit covariates)

Lastly, while I am working in the PointedSDMs package, I would also appreciate answers that tackle this issue for general inla/inlabru.

Many thanks in advance,
Moritz

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Generating a large mesh with holes - performance issues?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Generating a large mesh with holes - performance issues?
messages.body_plain:
Whether polygons are treated as holes or as "inverted holes" is
determined by the winding order. The convention in fmesher is that
"inside is to the left" when walking along the polygon boundary. That
means that a counterclockwise order is a regular domain boundary,
whereas clockwise order creates a hole. The sf standard essentially
works like that as well (but the sf package does not, as it often
calls the "libproj" library that has the opposite convention, and sf
neglects to convert back to the sf standard definition. So in practice
one may need some experimentation to get the intended behaviour). But
for the barrier method, you _don't_ want the islands to create holes;
you may just want the triangle edges to follow the island coastlines,
which can be achieved by specifying them using the "interior" argument
in the mesh creation.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatiotemporal model with dynamic covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

how to handle spatio-temporally variable covariates depends on the
storage format, and will also be different for georeferenced data and
for point pattern models; the former just needs the covariate values
to be available for each observation row in the data set. For point
pattern models, bru() with model="cp" or lgcp() in inlabru, the
covariate needs to evaluable at every location of the likelihood
integration construction, which typically means providing it as a
terra object, with one layer per time point, so that inlabru can
evaluate the needed values internally, or alternatively explicitly
call eval_spatial() to generate the component input values:
Either
  temperature(temperature_as_terra_object, main_selector = "month", ...)
or equivalently
  temperature(eval_spatial(temperature_as_terra_object, .data.,
selector = "month"), ...)
This approach works both for georeferenced and for point pattern
models, if the covariate is available as a terra raster (also see
?eval_spatial or
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/reference/eval_spatial.html for
what other storage formats are supported).
Some more info is available in the help text for bru_component,
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/reference/bru_component.html

I don't know enough about the PointedSDMs internals to know whether
this also works in that wrapper package.

Finn

On Tue, 11 Mar 2025 at 15:38, Moritz Klaassen <moritz....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi folks,
>
> I'm working on a marine integrated species distribution model (ISDM) using inlabru and the PointedSDMs wrapper. My model combines two data sources:
>
> Presence-Only (PO) Data:
> Collected over 12 months, this dataset is highly spatially biased but provides valuable temporal information on dynamic covariates (temperature).
>
> Presence-Absence (PA) Data:
> Derived from a survey (1 month)  with good spatial coverage, providing static covariates such as bathymetry and slope.
>
> My goal is to build an integrated model that incorporates bathymetry and slope from the PA data and temperature from the PO data, in which I want to model PO as an IPP and PA Binomial. To test whether the model can capture the dynamic distribution driven by temperature variations, I’m currently focusing on modelling only the PO data.
>
> In my workflow, I define the temporal component by including a "month" variable in the PO dataset. In the startISDM() call, I specify the temporal variable as follows:
>
> organizedData_PO <- startISDM(
>   data = po_sf,
>   Mesh = mesh,
>   Projection = proj_azores,
>   spatialCovariates = env_stack_bst_masked,
>   Boundary = boundary_inner_PO,
>   responseCounts = "counts",
>   pointsSpatial = "individual",
>   temporalName = "month"
> )
>
> For temperature, I combine the 12 monthly layers into a dynamic component using changeComponents(): (I also use a 1D SPDE for temperature to capture a non linear response)
>
> organizedData_PO$changeComponents(
>   "temperature(
>      main = I(
>       (month == 1)*temperature_month1 +
>       (month == 2)*temperature_month2 +
>       (month == 3)*temperature_month3 +
>       (month == 4)*temperature_month4 +
>       (month == 5)*temperature_month5 +
>       (month == 6)*temperature_month6 +
>       (month == 7)*temperature_month7 +
>       (month == 8)*temperature_month8 +
>       (month == 9)*temperature_month9 +
>       (month == 10)*temperature_month10 +
>       (month == 11)*temperature_month11 +
>       (month == 12)*temperature_month12
>      ),
>      model = INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(
>        mesh = fmesher::fm_mesh_1d(
>          loc      = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 20),
>          boundary = 'free'
>        ),
>        alpha       = 2,
>        prior.range = c(1, 0.05),
>        prior.sigma = c(1, 0.05),
>        constr      = TRUE
>      )
>   )"
> )
>
> However, I'm not entirely sure if this is the most elegant or robust way to link the temporal "month" variable from the PO sf to the dynamic temperature SPDE fields. I am wondering:
>
> Is specifying temporalName = "month" in startISDM() sufficient for linking the month-specific temperature layers to the PO data? (this question might be limited to users of the package)
> Are there any resources or example cases available where others have used temporally changing covariates in spatiotemporal models in INLA? (I am aware of a few examples using spatiotemporal models but not with temporally explicit covariates)
>
> Lastly, while I am working in the PointedSDMs package, I would also appreciate answers that tackle this issue for general inla/inlabru.
>
> Many thanks in advance,
> Moritz

Hi folks,

I hope you're all keeping well.

I'm running a model of skate presence (very zero-inflated, across the NE Atlantic shelf, this has become the story of my life at this point).

To validate the model I'm running a simulation study (according to Zuur et al., 2017) to simulate 1000 response datasets from model betas, and then compare the number of zeros in the simulated datasets with that of the observed data.

For the initial model formulation (f1), the observed zeros are right in the middle of the histogram of simulated zero counts (no problems there)

U <- 1 # priors for the temporal component, start with 1 and see how it looks. It worked ok this time
hyper.prec.year = list(theta = list(
  prior = "pc.prec",
  param = c(U, 0.01)))

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA Users,

I couldn't find if this had been answered before but my question seems related to these two recent questions: https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/1aiz-b0lHBA, https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/fzCkQ9Adwb4.

I'm trying to analyze fish distributions on patch reefs (effectively islands) as it relates to some environmental covariates (eg. rugosity) separated by large unsurveyed areas. The unsurveyed areas aren't appropriate habitat but unsurveyed which to me suggests that the "plot sampling" gorilla example (https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_plotsampling.html) is not the appropriate method to use here since that appears to say that the unsurveyed areas are still able to have gorillas they just weren't studied. In essence the reefs are islands and the areas between reefs is the ocean. The scale of the reefs surveyed is on the order of 10 x 20m with the distance between reefs ranging from ~100m to ~20km.

My first thought is to model these reefs as distinct islands each with their own mesh and spde model but a single effect for the spatial covariates. Is that possible? I'm trying to setup the model using inlabru and am running into problems trying to have site specific domains/spatial meshes and spde models.

Another possibility seems to be to create one large mesh over everything and then pluck out the islands by setting the areas between to a barrier and using that approach similar to the suggestion here: https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/fzCkQ9Adwb4. Does this work since the sites are entirely disconnected? All the examples I can find are of coastlines where the non-barrier areas are all connected.

Thanks for any thoughts/advice,
Jason

messages.subject: Questions about Delta/Hurdle Gamma model
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks

I’m currently self-studying spatial modeling but struggling to find the right approach.

My dependent variable is a right-skewed continuous variable with a high proportion of zeros (over 50%, n = 3,045 counties). The geometry data comes from the US Census data from tidycensus package, and it is stored as an sfc or sf object (seemingly polygons).

Given the high proportion of zeros, I believe a hurdle model is appropriate. While I plan to examine both spatial and temporal effects in the future, I am currently focusing only on the spatial effects for a single year. My goal is to determine whether there is a diffusion effect in the IV, DV, or error term.

I attempted to use sdmTMB to fit a hurdle Gamma model following this page (https://pbs-assess.github.io/sdmTMB/articles/delta-models.html) but encountered several challenges:

1. sdmTMB seems to be useful for point data. Would it be appropriate to extract coordinates from the polygons and convert them into point data for estimation?

2. I tried using sanity() to assess model fit, but it resulted in an error. Could this indicate that my data is problematic?

3. When I apply a log(x+1) transformation to the DV, the nonzero values become approximately normally distributed. Should I log-transform the DV before running a Gamma hurdle model?

df.g <- st_read("all23.g.gpkg")
df.g <- df.g |> na.omit()
centroids <- st_centroid(df.g)

centroid_coords <- st_coordinates(centroids)
pcod <- data.frame(X = centroid_coords[, 1],
                   Y = centroid_coords[, 2])

mesh <- make_mesh(pcod, c("X", "Y"), cutoff = 15)

df.drop <- df.g %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

fit_dg <- sdmTMB(solpckwk ~ edu + hsp + blk + incmk,
                 data = df.drop,
                 mesh = mesh,
                 family = delta_gamma(),
                 spatial = list("on", "on"))

print(fit_dg)

I also attempted to estimate Spatial Error Models and Spatial Lag Models using lagsarlm() and errorsarlm() from the spatialreg package (I referred to this page: https://walker-data.com/census-r/spatial-analysis-with-us-census-data.html#spatial-subsets-and-spatial-predicates). However, when I drop zeros, more than half of the regions lose their neighbors, causing the code to fail.

4. Would modifying the spatial weights matrix allow lagsarlm() or errorsarlm() to work in this case? I generated the spatial weights matrix using this code, defining adjacency in a queen contiguity scheme:

wts <- df %>%
  poly2nb() %>%
  nb2listw()

I’d greatly appreciate any advice!

Best,
Joo

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: LGCP analysis of Islands. Mesh creation
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: LGCP analysis of Islands. Mesh creation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I did a quick check of the code, and the problem is that you're giving
a list of spde model objects to the model instead of a single spde
object:

#### spde model ####
reef_spde <- map(reef_mesh,
                 ~inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = .x,
                                      prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
                                      prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)))

#### Prep model ####
components <- geometry ~ Intercept(1) +
  site(main = site, model = "iid") +
  spatial_field(geometry,
                model = reef_spde,
                replicate = site_idx)

Since you're asking for an independent replicate for each separate
site, what you really need is a single mesh for the combination of all
the sites. As that mesh will consist of disconnected components (if
the sites are far enough apart, and if they are close it makes more
sense for them to actually be connected; see example code below), they
will have independent values but the same range/sigma parameters, just
as you intended.
Also, your "cp" samplers need to be the reef boundaries, not the entire mesh.
The code below hopefully gives you a pointer in the right direction.

reef_mesh_combined <- fm_mesh_2d(
  boundary = list(
    reef_boundaries$geometry,
    fm_nonconvex_hull(reef_boundaries$geometry, 10)
  ),
  max.edge = c(2, 50),
  cutoff = 0.5,
  offset = c(1, 3),
  crs = fm_crs(newproj)
)

ggplot() +
  gg(reef_mesh_combined) +
  geom_sf(data = shoal_locations)

#### spde model ####
reef_spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = reef_mesh_combined,
                                      prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
                                      prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)))

#### Prep model ####
components <- geometry ~ Intercept(1) +
  site(main = site, model = "iid") +
  spatial_field(geometry,
                model = reef_spde)

# Note: This doesn't need to be precomputed, as it keeps the site information
# in the integration points; the domain and samplers can be given to
# bru()/bru_obs() instead:
integration_points <- fm_int(domain = list(geometry = reef_mesh_combined,
                                           site = unique(reef_boundaries$site)),
                             samplers = reef_boundaries)

#### Fit Model ####
fit_location <- bru(formula = geometry ~ Intercept + site + spatial_field,
                    components = components,
                    data = shoal_locations,
                    family = "cp",
                    ips = integration_points,
                    options = list(verbose = TRUE))

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] assessing model performance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bram,

since CPO = Pr(Y_i|Y_{not i}) according to the estimated model, then values in the (0.00,0.011) can be entirely reasonable for discrete data;
For example, consider an outcome of 200 when the estimated posterior conditional prediction model is Binomial(1000, 0.2), i.e. the observed value is equal to the expectation, and thus should be consider a good prediction.
The CPO is then
> dbinom(200,1000,0.2)
[1] 0.03152536
You cannot interpret CPO values outside the context of what the model is (discrete/continuous, overall size etc), and the main use is to compare _different_ models for the same data. Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] assessing model performance
messages.body_plain:
It depends on what aspect of the model performance you're interested in. CPO does "what it says on the tin", and one just has to interpret the values accordingly; when the possibly discrete value outcomes number in the thousands, and there is inherent randomness in the observation stage, then one simply can't expect large prediction probabilities. One option is to use other proper scores such as squared error or absolute error. What is useful depends entirely on your specific problem. In other words, think about what _you_ care about, and find a metric that evaluates that. This also involved choosing something other than "leave-one-out" prediction, but e.g. using group-cv doesn't remove the issue of what metric to evaluate for such group-leave-out predictions.

Finn

messages.subject: Role of "phi" in multinomial logit models for spatial random effect
messages.subject_clean: Role of "phi" in multinomial logit models for spatial random effect
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA-users,

I am trying to estimate rates of choices in a space according to this text (https://inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/doc/vignettes/multinomial.pdf). In this estimation, I and my collaborator are confused with the role of "phi" in page 2 and 8 of the above text.

The question is: Are these "phi" necessary for Poisson trick? Or are they necessary only for improper models?

When I test models without phi, they work well for besagproper and besagproper2 and do not well for besag, besag2 and SPDE.
When I test a model with phi, it works well for besag and besag2 and does not for besagproper and besagproper2 (not yet tested on SPDE).

The tested models are like these:

Models without phi:
formula<-Y~ -1 + f(alt1, model="besagproper")
models[[1]]<-inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data1, control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))
formula<-Y~ -1 + f(alt2, model="besagproper")
models[[2]]<-inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data2, control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))
formula<-Y~ -1 + f(alt3, model="besagproper")
models[[3]]<-inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data3, control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))

Model with phi:
formula<-Y~ -1 + f(alt1, model="besag") + f(alt2, model="besag") + f(alt3, model="besag") + f(phi,initial=-10,fixed=T)
model<-inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data, control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE), control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"))

The goals of these estimation are such as alt1/(alt1+alt2+al3) and their CIs.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Satoshi Aoki

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Role of "phi" in multinomial logit models for spatial random effect
messages.body_plain:
The multinomial likelihood has dependiencies between the number of counts in the
1..m slots. We can rewrite this as conditional independent poisson counts as
long as we make the linear predictors dependent by introducing \phi_i, which has
one value for each observation vector. The proof is there on page 2-3, and is
'well known'.

we can use a similar trick in Compositional Data Analysis as well

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-024-10427-3

    Ysim[,i]    <- rnbinom(n = length(mu), size= size, mu=mu)
}

predictions <- inla.posterior.sample.eval("APredictor", SimData)
predictions <- predictions[1:1307,] #sample locations

Satoshi Aoki
2025年3月18日火曜日 16:50:19 UTC+9 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue):

>
> The multinomial likelihood has dependiencies between the number of counts in the
> 1..m slots. We can rewrite this as conditional independent poisson counts as
> long as we make the linear predictors dependent by introducing \phi_i, which has
> one value for each observation vector. The proof is there on page 2-3, and is
> 'well known'.
>
> we can use a similar trick in Compositional Data Analysis as well
>
> https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-024-10427-3
>
>
>
> On Mon, 2025-03-17 at 18:09 -0700, Satoshi Aoki wrote:
> > Dear INLA-users,
> >
> > I am trying to estimate rates of choices in a space according to this text
> > (https://inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/doc/vignettes/multinomial.pdf).
> > In this estimation, I and my collaborator are confused with the role of "phi"
> > in page 2 and 8 of the above text.
> >
> > The question is: Are these "phi" necessary for Poisson trick? Or are they
> > necessary only for improper models?
> >
> > When I test models without phi, they work well for besagproper and
> > besagproper2 and do not well for besag, besag2 and SPDE.
> > When I test a model with phi, it works well for besag and besag2 and does not
> > for besagproper and besagproper2 (not yet tested on SPDE).
> >
> > The tested models are like these:
> >
> > Models without phi:
> > formula<-Y~ -1 + f(alt1, model="besagproper")
> > models[[1]]<-inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data1,
> > control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),control.predictor =
> > list(compute=TRUE))
> > formula<-Y~ -1 + f(alt2, model="besagproper")
> > models[[2]]<-inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data2,
> > control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),control.predictor =
> > list(compute=TRUE))
> > formula<-Y~ -1 + f(alt3, model="besagproper")
> > models[[3]]<-inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data3,
> > control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),control.predictor =
> > list(compute=TRUE))
> >
> > Model with phi:
> > formula<-Y~ -1 + f(alt1, model="besag") + f(alt2, model="besag") + f(alt3,

> > model<-inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data,
> > control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),control.predictor =
> > list(compute=TRUE), control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"))
> >
> > The goals of these estimation are such as alt1/(alt1+alt2+al3) and their CIs.

vignette about why this is the thing to do...)

let me know

best
H

messages.subject: help need
messages.body_plain:
i want to do a spatial analysis on perinatal deaths at the commune level. my dependent variable is binary and a commune can be repeated more than once because deaths are observed at the cluster level. so a commune can contain several clusters. i want to use bayesian modeling with a binomial distribution.
my concern is that i have an imbalance in my dependent variable which represents death (3% for class1 and 97% for class0). i wanted to know if i should make corrections with the bayesian modeling or what are the possible approaches.

Translated with DeepL.com (free version)

this is my model :
f4 <- cm_peri ~ f(ID, model = "bym2", graph = g, constr = TRUE, scale.model = TRUE, hyper = hyper_bym2) +
  residence + education+ niveau_vie+statut_mat + ìntervalle_naissance + sexe_enfant+f(gr_age_mere_naissance,model="iid")+ ordre_naissance+lieu_soins+ Distance_m

###  ajustement du  modele
mod4b <- inla(
  f4,
  family = "binomial",  # Utilisation de la famille binomiale pour la variable binaire
  data = base,
  #weights = base$v005,  # Ajouter les pondérations dans le modèle
  control.fixed = control.fixed,  # Prior sur les coefficients de régression
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),  # Calcul des prédictions
  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, config = TRUE, return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),  # Calcul des critères DIC et WAIC
  control.inla = list(strategy = "laplace")  # Stratégie d'approximation
)

#####
# Résumé des résultats
summary(mod4b)

messages.body_plain:
Or use the inla.spde2.pcmatern() model, which is defined for both 2D and 1D; use fmesher::fm_mesh_1d() to define the temporal space. The basic implementation allows alpha=1 and alpha=2 (smoothness like rw1 and rw2, but with matern covariance instead) as well as approximations for fractional orders. For fractional orders, the rSPDE package has better approximations than inla.spde2.pcmatern, for both 1D and 2D.

Finn
